marble.name: Mass vs Weight
marble.subject: Science
marble.description: Distinguish between mass (amount of matter, measured in kg) and weight (gravitational force, measured in N), use the equation weight = mass × gravitational field strength, and explain why g differs on other planets and stars
marble.prompt: If you weighed themselves on bathroom scales and was then asked what they would weigh on the Moon, could they explain the difference between mass and weight and work out a rough answer?

cluster.summary: Your child is learning about forces — understanding how pushes and pulls can make objects move faster, slower, or change direction, and testing different ways to affect motion.

misconceptions: Mass and weight are interchangeable words for the same property (the core error; ~56% define weight as 'heavy or light'; persists into adulthood)
Weight is a fixed property of the object that doesn't change with location — or, conversely, that mass AND weight both shrink equally on the Moon
Confusing the units — treating kg as a unit of weight/force (reinforced by grocery packaging putting grams beside force units)
A balance and a spring scale 'measure the same thing'
Entangled gravity errors: no gravity in space → no weight and no mass; gravity needs air
representations: Same object on a balance (reads kg, unchanged) beside a spring scale/newton meter (reads N) — two readings, two quantities
Planet/Moon 'weigh-station' comparison table: mass constant, weight scaling with g
W = m × g shown as a proportional relationship with units flagged (ratio table across planets)
authoredAnswer: Its mass stays the same (6 kg) — mass is the amount of matter, which doesn't depend on location. Its weight DECREASES — weight is the gravitational force on it (W = mg), and the Moon's gravitational field strength g is about a sixth of Earth's, so the rock weighs about a sixth as much. So weight changes, mass doesn't.

wrongAnswers.wrong: Its mass gets smaller too, because it's lighter on the Moon.
wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Changes the mass along with the weight.
wrongAnswers.fix: Operational split: a balance (comparing amounts of matter) reads the same on the Moon; a spring force-meter reads less. Mass = matter, weight = the pull.

wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Uses kg and N interchangeably and can't say which one changes.
wrongAnswers.fix: Mass in kg on a balance (same everywhere); weight in N on a force-meter (changes with g). Give each its own instrument.

wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Says the weight is zero on the Moon.
wrongAnswers.fix: The Moon HAS gravity, about a sixth of Earth's, so weight is reduced, not zero — astronauts still stand on the surface.
